result: Cell surface PDI (csPDI) was identified in chick somites through biochemical purification and mass spectrometry, revealing a 57 kDa O-glycosylated protein that binds PNA and is expressed at the surface of P-half-sclerotome cells.
evaluation: Claims C16-C17 provide mass spectrometry identification of PDI from PNA-purified somite extracts. Claims C20, C22-C23 demonstrate O-glycosylation through PNA binding properties and confirm cell surface localization through live-staining and co-localization experiments. The convergence of biochemical, proteomic, and immunofluorescence data strongly supports this identification.

result: The onset of csPDI expression in P-half-sclerotome precedes the first emergence of motor and sensory axon outgrowth in the A-half-sclerotome by approximately 1.5-3 hours.
evaluation: Claims C24 and C75 are supported by temporal analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c,d, demonstrating that PNA staining (indicating csPDI expression) appears before axon outgrowth. This temporal relationship is consistent with a causal role for csPDI in axon guidance.

result: siRNA knockdown of PDI in ovo caused loss of PNA-binding in P-half-sclerotomes and resulted in abnormal motor axon projections into P-half-sclerotomes, with partial rescue by co-injection of human PDIA1 plasmid.
evaluation: Claims C25-C26 demonstrate the phenotypic consequences of PDI knockdown with appropriate controls (scrambled siRNA). Claims C27-C28 show that somite polarity markers are largely unaffected, ruling out gross developmental defects. Claim C29 provides rescue data that strengthens the specificity of the knockdown effect. Together, these claims provide strong in vivo evidence for PDI's role in axon guidance.

result: Pharmacological inhibition of PDI activity using PACMA 31 (but not control PACMA 56) caused abnormal axon projections into P-half-sclerotomes and increased ventral root width, both by direct injection and bead implantation.
evaluation: Claims C30-C34 demonstrate that specific inhibition of PDI enzymatic activity (C30) produces phenotypes similar to genetic knockdown. The use of an inactive control compound (PACMA 56) and quantification of effects (C32-C34) strengthen the conclusion. Multiple delivery methods (injection and bead implantation) increase confidence in the findings.

result: Purified PDI alone does not induce growth cone collapse, but PDI combined with GSNO (1 μM) causes significant collapse (~60% after 1 hour) with similar concentration dependence and time course whether applied in solution or liposomes.
evaluation: Claims C35-C37 establish that PDI requires a co-factor (GSNO) to induce collapse, ruling out direct PDI-receptor interactions. Claims C38-C39 demonstrate consistency across different assay formats and distinguish the PDI+GSNO response from other repellents (Sema3A). This is well-supported by dose-response and time-course data.

result: Multiple PDI inhibitors (bacitracin, anti-PDI antibody, PAO, and PACMA 31) reduce PDI+GSNO-induced or somite extract-induced growth cone collapse.
evaluation: Claims C40-C41 demonstrate that chemically diverse PDI inhibitors block collapse activity, providing pharmacological validation of PDI's role. The use of multiple inhibitors with different mechanisms strengthens the conclusion and rules out off-target effects of any single compound.

result: PDI can be S-nitrosylated and acts as a denitrosylase, with GSH (but not DTT or L-homocysteine) blocking collapse activity at 3 mM but not at physiological extracellular concentrations (3 μM).
evaluation: Claims C43-C45 establish the biochemical mechanism from prior literature. Claims C46-C49 demonstrate that the authors' experimental system recapitulates this mechanism with appropriate specificity for GSH. The concentration-dependence (C48) is critical for physiological relevance. The data are internally consistent and well-controlled.

result: NO scavengers (myoglobin and C-PTIO) inhibit collapse induced by PDI+GSNO and somite extracts, and the nNOS inhibitor L-NAME (but not D-NAME) prevents somite extract-induced collapse.
evaluation: Claims C50-C52 provide multiple lines of evidence that NO signaling is required for collapse. The use of membrane-impermeable scavengers (C51) and stereoisomer controls (C52) strengthens the conclusions. These data support the proposed mechanism involving NO transfer and amplification.

result: LC1 (MAP1B light chain, 38 kDa) is the only major S-nitrosylated protein detected in somite extracts, and its S-nitrosylation is blocked by L-NAME but not D-NAME.
evaluation: Claims C54-C55 identify LC1 as the S-nitrosylated target using iodo-TMT labeling and Western blotting. Claim C56 demonstrates nNOS-dependence with appropriate stereoisomer controls. Claim C87 confirms the specificity of LC1 as the predominant target. The identification of a single major target is remarkable and well-supported by the data.

result: Rat forebrain extracts (RFE) contain PDI-dependent collapse activity that is depleted by jacalin, inhibited by PACMA 31, quercetin-3-O-rutinoside, anti-PDI antibody, GSH (3 mM), and NO scavengers.
evaluation: Claims C58-C64 demonstrate that mammalian brain tissue contains a collapse activity with properties identical to somite csPDI. Multiple orthogonal approaches (lectin depletion, pharmacological inhibition, immunodepletion, reducing agents, NO scavengers) all point to the same mechanism. The dose-response data (C63) strengthen the conclusions.

result: csPDI is expressed on the surface of cultured human astrocytic cells and rat cortical astrocytes, and astrocyte extracts cause collapse that is depleted by PNA and jacalin.
evaluation: Claims C66-C68 identify astrocytes as a source of brain csPDI through live-staining (C66), functional assays (C67), and biochemical isolation (C68). The convergence of immunofluorescence, collapse assays, and Western blotting provides strong support for astrocytic expression of functional csPDI.

result: Chick retinal axon growth cones collapse in response to both somite extracts and PDI+GSNO.
evaluation: Claims C71-C72 demonstrate that CNS neurons (retinal) respond to the csPDI system, extending the findings beyond PNS neurons. Claim C71 is supported by both current data and prior citation, while C72 provides new confirmatory data. This supports the broader relevance of the mechanism.

result: The authors propose a mechanism in which csPDI acts as a denitrosylase at the P-half-somite cell surface, transferring NO from extracellular S-nitrosothiols (GSNO at ~1 μM) into growth cone filopodia, leading to LC1 S-nitrosylation, enhanced MAP1B-microtubule binding, dynein blockade, and growth cone collapse.
evaluation: Claim C82 presents the overall mechanistic model, which is supported by the experimental data throughout the paper. Claim C84 demonstrates that physiologically relevant GSNO concentrations are sufficient. Claims C85-C86 integrate prior mechanistic work (Stroissnigg et al.) with the current findings. The model is well-supported by the convergence of biochemical, pharmacological, and cell biological data, though some steps remain inferential.

result: Neural crest cell and axon segmental patterning are regulated by distinct molecular signals: Semaphorin/Ephrin signaling affects neural crest but not axons, while PDI affects axons.
evaluation: Claims C79-C81 synthesize prior literature showing that genetic disruption of Semaphorin/Ephrin signaling affects neural crest but leaves axon patterning intact. This supports the inference (C80) that distinct mechanisms regulate these two cell types. The logic is sound and well-supported by cited evidence.

result: Background: In avian and mammalian embryos, motor and sensory axons traverse anterior half-somites through contact repulsion mediated by P-half-somite factors. Previous work identified PNA-binding glycoproteins (48 and 55 kDa) with collapse-inducing activity.
evaluation: Claims C1, C7-C15 establish the biological context and prior work from the authors' laboratory. These are well-supported by multiple citations and represent established knowledge in the field. This background is essential for understanding the significance of the current findings.

result: Background: PDI/PDIA1/P4HB is a thioredoxin-fold protein family member, principally known as an ER enzyme that catalyzes disulfide bond formation/breakage. PDI has two active sites (WCGHCK) and can be expressed at the cell surface in O-glycosylated form.
evaluation: Claims C18-C19, C21, and C42 provide essential background on PDI structure and function, supported by appropriate citations. This established knowledge contextualizes the novel finding of csPDI's role in axon guidance.

result: Background: S-nitrosylation of Cys 2457 in MAP1B LC1 is critical for growth cone collapse, as shown by Stroissnigg et al. (2007).
evaluation: Claim C53 accurately represents prior work that provides the mechanistic framework for interpreting the current findings. This is well-supported by citation and is critical for the proposed mechanism.

result: Background: Astrocytes share SOX9 fate specification with P-half-sclerotome cells. NGF-dependent sensory neurons project to CNS. CNS neurons respond to somite repellents. Contact between growth cone filopodia and P-half-somite cells triggers rapid repulsion. PDI knockdown does not affect cell viability.
evaluation: Claims C65, C69-C70, C73-C74, C76-C78 provide relevant background information supported by appropriate citations. These contextual claims help interpret the significance of the findings but are not primary results of the current study.

result: Speculation: GSNO may provide a ubiquitous NO donor source. A broad range of CNS axon types may be susceptible to csPDI-mediated repulsion. csPDI may be bifunctional in promoting both adhesive and repulsive interactions. csPDI might provide an extracellular NO source during synapse elimination.
evaluation: Claims C83, C88, C92, and C94 are explicitly speculative statements about potential broader implications and future directions. While these are reasonable hypotheses based on the data, they require additional experimental validation and are appropriately presented as speculation by the authors.

result: Background: csPDI has been implicated in glioblastoma invasiveness, identified at CNS synapses and on neuroblastoma/retinal cells, and NO signaling is implicated in synapse elimination.
evaluation: Claims C89-C91, C93 cite prior literature showing diverse roles and locations of csPDI in the nervous system. These are well-supported by citations and provide context for the potential broader significance of the findings.
